title: Depth First Search (DFS) Explained: Algorithm, Examples, and Code
beats: Four-part plan: traversal concept, invent your own, implementation, applications
Graph traversal = visit every vertex from a start; algorithms differ in order
Let's invent a traversal: pick any unvisited neighbour, go on
Walk a 10-vertex graph aloud: go deeper, hit dead end, retrace; 2:49-4:11 repeated backtracks
Think of yourself as a bold adventurous explorer who retraces at dead ends
Second valid ordering, different choices; exams specify tie-breaking (smaller first)
Move to a smaller graph for implementation; notice it is naturally recursive
First recursion attempt; 'pause, find the bug'; infinite loop via vertex 0
Fix with marked/boolean list; trace the recursion call by call
Iterative version with stack; trace including duplicates on stack
Both O(V+E); recursive is standard, iterative generalises to other traversals
Pre-order vs post-order; post-order is moving the visit call to the end
Topological sort; reverse post-order; 'think why' left to viewer
Maze generation: randomised neighbour order; try solving it

metrics.ending: Applications montage ending on a playful maze, no strong recap

new_moves.name: invent-then-name
new_moves.what: Derive the algorithm by narration before the name is given, then state 'this is exactly DFS'

new_moves.name: shrink-for-implementation
new_moves.what: Switch to a smaller graph when moving from concept to code to reduce moving parts

new_moves.name: deliberate-bug-then-fix
new_moves.what: Show naive implementation, ask viewer to find flaw, then patch

theory: The video teaches DFS as something the viewer could have invented: a long literal walk establishes the intuition, and only later does code appear as a transcription of that behaviour. The buggy first draft turns the visited array into a discovered fix rather than a given rule.
velocity: Playbook: 'invent-then-name' for algorithms, with ghost hands tracing the walk and the name revealed only after the second repetition
Scene builder: auto-generate a small graph from a large one when the concept switches to code
Learner model: pause and ask the learner to predict the bug in a naive version before showing it
Evals: algorithm name should not appear before the first full literal walkthrough
quote: think of yourself as a bold and adventurous explorer
